extraction.paper_summary: This is a review paper on aluminum matrix syntactic foams (AMSFs), covering fabrication routes (pressure/counter-gravity/gas-vacuum infiltration, stir/centrifugal/buoyancy dispersion casting), macro/micro structure, densities of published foams (Table 3), and compressive mechanical properties compiled from the literature (Table 4), plus prospective automotive/aerospace applications. Reported foam densities span ~0.7-2.3 g/cm3 and compressive strengths from ~37 MPa up to ~190 MPa quasi-statically (572 MPa reported for a dynamic Al2014/cenosphere case). No new experiments are performed; all data are literature compilations.

extraction.extraction_notes: This is a review; all records are literature-compiled values from Table 4 (mechanical) cross-referenced with Table 3 (densities) by citation number. sigma_com (1% offset yield stress per ISO 13314) was mapped to strength_mpa; sigma_plt to plateau_stress_mpa; eps_den to densification_strain. '*' entries in Table 4 mean not reported and were left null. Strain rates were not given numerically ('quasi-static' vs 'dynamic' only), so strain_rate_per_s is null and the distinction is captured in specimen_notes. Densities reported as ranges in Table 3 were not assigned to specific records (left null, noted in microstructure_notes); only the single-valued density (A356/SiC, 1.81 g/cm3) was used. Particle sizes given as ranges were left null in particle_mean_diameter_um; single values (1 mm, 3 mm) were converted to µm and entered, though the paper lists them as filler sizes rather than mean diameters. Process routes were assigned only where the review's text or reference titles state them; otherwise 'other'. Counter-gravity infiltration ([5],[19]) was mapped to pressure_infiltration; microwave sintering ([61]) to powder_metallurgy. Volume/weight fractions of fillers are not reported in this review.

extraction.paper_summary: The paper studies elastomeric syntactic foams made of a Sylgard 184 PDMS matrix filled with 3M A16-500 borosilicate glass microballoons (GMB) at 10-46.2 vol%, combining cyclic uniaxial compression experiments, analytic composite theory (equivalent solid-sphere + Christensen composite spheres), and finite element homogenization of RVEs. It compares undamaged, fully debonded, and fully crushed GMB states, finding that the composite bulk modulus is drastically reduced by crushed GMBs (even 5% crushed number fraction) but nearly insensitive to debonding, while the shear modulus is reduced by both mechanisms. Debonding also produces tension-compression asymmetry and loss of major symmetry of the homogenized stiffness tensor.

Neat matrix (unfilled Sylgard 184) properties from Table 2 (K = 920 MPa, E = 2.52 MPa, mu = 0.84 MPa, nu = 0.4995) are reference constituent data, not a syntactic foam composition, and were not entered as a record. Weight and volume fractions converted from percent to fractions. Test temperature recorded as 25 C ('room temperature'). Numerical/FEA parametric results (normalized moduli vs. volume fraction, radius ratio, crushed fraction) are only presented as normalized plots and were not extracted. Radius ratio 0.9667 is the nominal value stated for the A16 GMBs used.

extraction.paper_summary: The paper characterises Al7075-T aluminium matrix syntactic foams made by pressure infiltration casting with ceramic hollow microspheres (66 vol.%, 88 wt.%) in three size ranges (25-75, 100-250, 250-500 um), tested under quasi-static compression, Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar, ballistic impact and blast loading. Quasi-static plastic collapse stress ranged from 75-179 MPa (densities 1585-2388 kg/m3), while dynamic compressive strengths reached 203-601 MPa at strain rates of 882-1578 1/s, showing strong rate sensitivity above 1000 1/s. Concrete Damage Plasticity FE models reproduced compression, ballistic and blast responses and predicted a 20 mm thickness is needed to arrest a 7.62x39 mm projectile at 750 m/s.

extraction.extraction_notes: Moduli converted from GPa to MPa; densities from kg/m3 to g/cm3; densification strains from % to fraction. Quasi-static strain rate was not stated explicitly; it was computed as 1 mm/min crosshead on a 20 mm specimen ~= 8.3e-4 1/s. Table 4 (SHPB) gives only relative densities (rho/rho_s with rho_s = 2810 kg/m3 for Al7075-T6); these differ slightly from the Table 3 bulk densities, so measured density was left null for the dynamic records and recorded in microstructure_notes. Particle mean diameters were not reported (only size ranges 25-75, 100-250, 250-500 um for CM(I)-CM(III)); left null. Specific energy absorption vs strain rate is only shown graphically (Fig. 11a), so no numeric values extracted. Ballistic (Tables 5-6: depth of penetration, residual velocity) and blast (Table 7: impulse, mid-point deflection) results do not map to the schema property fields and were not converted into records; the reported 66 vol.% / 88 wt.% microsphere content and Al7075-T matrix apply to all specimens.

extraction.paper_summary: Injection-molded PP/EPR syntactic foams with 10 vol% pores made either from Expancel PMMA microballoons (Balloon 80, Balloon 120; spherical pores) or supercritical CO2 gas foaming (Gas 50, Gas 250; elliptical pores) were tensile tested at 0.3-100 1/s and dart-impact tested at 0.1-10 m/s, and modelled with a craze-evolution constitutive law and microstructural FE. Elastic modulus was unaffected by pore shape; yield stress and strain energy dropped more for gas-foamed (elliptical) pores, and microballoon foams absorbed about 1.4x more dart-impact energy than SCF gas foams.

extraction.extraction_notes: Only the two microballoon-filled materials (Balloon 80/120) are hollow-particle composites; the SCF gas-foamed PP (Gas 50/250) and neat PP references are not and were not recorded. All quantitative mechanical results (apparent elastic modulus, yield stress, rupture strain, strain energy up to failure vs strain rate in Figs. 9-12; dart maximum load and absorbed energy in Figs. 14-15) are shown only as plots with no numeric values in text or tables, so property fields are left null; records carry composition/process/test metadata only. Text states modulus of microballoon shell ~2 GPa and neat PP E = 800 MPa, sigma_y,neat = 17.432 MPa (model parameters, Table 2) - not foam properties. Relative density 0.90 is a model input. Test temperature assumed room temperature. Records are per (material x test type); per-strain-rate splitting was not done because no per-rate values are readable.

extraction.paper_summary: Choqueuse et al. (IFREMER, 2010) describe test methods for hollow-glass-microsphere syntactic foams used as deep-sea pipeline thermal insulation: a buoyancy-based hydrostatic compression test giving bulk modulus and crush pressure, and Iosipescu / modified Arcan shear tests. An epoxy-matrix foam (Mat A) shows near-linear hydrostatic response with crush pressure ~90 MPa versus ~50 MPa for a polyurethane-matrix foam (Mat B) with the same microspheres; Mat A shear modulus ~800 MPa; Mat B is strongly rate-sensitive and cracks at ~120% shear strain. Temperature (4-100 C) strongly affects an epoxy foam (Mat C) but no numbers are given.

extraction.extraction_notes: Text is heavily duplicated by the PDF extraction (each paragraph repeated many times); content is a 6-page conference paper with no data tables. Microsphere grade, volume fraction, densities and manufacturing route are not specified (paper only says foams are made by co-extrusion, lateral extrusion or moulding), so process_route='other' and particle details are null. Fig. 3 values (bulk modulus 2.9 GPa, crush pressure 95 MPa) are for an unnamed 'typical' material, matrix unspecified (matrix_class='other'). For hydrostatic records, modulus_mpa holds the bulk modulus and strength_mpa the crush pressure. Mat C epoxy temperature study (4, 50, 100 C) and Mat B loading-rate study are only plotted, no numbers given, so not recorded. Iosipescu shear curves (Fig. 5) and Arcan strengths (Fig. 7) not read from plots.

extraction.paper_summary: de Lorgeril, Wyss and Orbulov (Periodica Polytechnica Mech. Eng. 2011) propose a mathematical description (modified Chesler-Cram peak function plus fifth-order polynomial) of the compressive engineering stress-strain curves of pressure-infiltrated aluminium matrix syntactic foams (Al99.5, AlSi12, AlMgSi1, AlCu5, AlZn5 matrices with 64 vol% Envirospheres SL150 or SL300 ceramic microballoons). 540 upsetting tests (three aspect ratios, three heat-treatment/temperature conditions) were fitted, and only qualitative trends of compressive strength, fracture strain, structural stiffness and absorbed energy versus H/D ratio are reported in the annex tables.
extraction.extraction_notes: FLAGGED FALSE PER RULE 10 (no quantitative hollow-particle composite data), although the subject IS metal matrix syntactic foam. The paper is clearly about metal matrix syntactic foams, but it reports NO numerical property values: compressive strength, fracture strain, stiffness and absorbed energy are shown only as trend words (increase/decrease/constant/hat/valley/unknown) in Tab. 4-7 and in unreadable Figs. 4-7. Therefore no records were created. Material descriptors available for future use: matrices Al99.5, AlSi12, AlMgSi1, AlCu5, AlZn5; microballoons Envirospheres SL150 (100 um average diameter, bulk density 0.576 g/cm3 at 64 vol%) and SL300 (150 um, 0.691 g/cm3 at 64 vol%), 30-35 wt% Al2O3 / 45-50 wt% amorphous SiO2 / 19 wt% mullite / 1 wt% quartz; 64 vol% microballoons in all cases; pressure infiltration; 14 mm diameter cylinders with H/D = 1, 1.5, 2; conditions ST 20 (solution treated, 20 C), HT 20 (T6, 20 C), ST 220 (solution treated, tested at 220 C); T6 parameters in Tab. 3. The 'Density (at 64 vol%)' column in Tab. 2 refers to the microballoon bed, not the foam.

extraction.paper_summary: Kozma et al. (Int. J. Computer Theory and Engineering 2015) present a CT-image-based 'radius incrementation' circle-fitting algorithm to reconstruct the outer surfaces of ceramic hollow spheres in an aluminium matrix syntactic foam specimen (15 x 22.5 mm cylinder, 900 CT slices at 7 um resolution) and build a CAD model for finite element analysis. Only image-fitting errors (1.0-1.5 % average) are reported; no processing, density or mechanical property data of the foam are given.
extraction.extraction_notes: The material studied is an Al matrix syntactic foam with ceramic spherical shells, but the paper is purely about the image-processing/reconstruction algorithm. No composition, volume fraction, density, or mechanical/thermal property values are reported, so there are no extractable records; flagged as not a syntactic-foam data paper per rule 10 (no hollow-particle composite data).

extraction.paper_summary: Yazici (Acta Physica Polonica A 2016) develops syntactic foams from a rigid two-part polyurethane casting resin (Smooth-On Task 3) toughened with 10 wt% silicone rubber (MoldStar30) and filled with 10, 30 or 50 wt% 3M A20/1000 glass bubbles (0.2 g/cm3, 105 um), cast by hand mixing into wax molds. Quasi-static compression (Instron, 1 mm/min) shows density and yield strength decreasing with GB content while the plateau region extends; split Hopkinson pressure bar tests (about 2800 1/s) show type B (30 wt% GB) foam has roughly eight times higher strength than under quasi-static loading.

extraction.paper_summary: Al-12Si syntactic foams were made by vacuum infiltration of a tap-packed bed (~65%) of 1-2 mm expanded soda-lime glass particles (EGP, 0.35 g/cm3) in stainless steel moulds preheated at 200-600 C. Foams had density ~1.14 g/cm3; mould preheats >=400 C caused clamping and EGP damage, lowering stiffness, 25%-strain crush strength and energy absorption but removing the yield load drop and raising energy absorption efficiency (84-88%). Liquid-nitrogen quenching of low-preheat samples produced the same effect; CTE was reduced to 17-19e-6/K for undamaged foams.

extraction.paper_summary: LM6 Al-Si alloy was vacuum-infiltrated at 700 C into packed beds (packing fraction 0.66-0.69) of 2-3 mm expanded soda-lime glass particles (EGP, 0.35 g/cc) to make syntactic metal foam beams and, in a single casting step, sandwich structures with integral Al-Si face sheets. Three-point bending gave a foam core Young's modulus of ~7007 MPa at 1.14 g/cc (power-law dependence on density, exponent ~2); FEA with this input matched sandwich stiffness within 1-3%, while the classical sandwich analytical model overestimated stiffness by 30-60% for thick faces; modelled mass savings of 11-31% versus solid Al.

extraction.paper_summary: Cheneler and Kennedy compare porous Al (salt-bead replication) with Al-Si (LM6) syntactic metal foams made by vacuum-assisted infiltration of packed beds of 2-3 mm porous expanded glass particles (EGP, 0.35 g/cc). SMFs with densities 1.00-1.19 g/cc were compression tested; stiffness, crush strength (stress at 0.25 strain) and energy absorption follow power laws in density with exponents near 3. EGP addition raises stiffness by ~2-3 GPa and crush strength by ~13 MPa relative to porous Al of equal metal fraction; FE modelling supports small reinforcement by the EGP.

extraction.paper_summary: Al 7075 matrix syntactic foams with 2-4 mm hollow bubble alumina spheres (Alodur KKW) were made by a recyclable gravity-assisted pressure infiltration casting (720 C, 0.1 MPa). Six cylindrical foams (density 1.72-1.78 g/cm3, filler 60-63 vol%, total porosity 43-46%) were compression tested at 1 mm/min per ISO 13314; three were T6 aged. extraction.paper_summary: Epoxy (E-51/100-1B) syntactic foams filled with 30 vol% 3M hollow glass microspheres (K1, S35, S60HS) were reinforced with warp-knitted spacer fabrics (B1-B4) to form 3DSMRC ternary composites, and compared with neat syntactic foam (NSF) under quasi-static compression (2 mm/min, 8 mm thick samples). Suitable WKSF (B1, B2, B4) raised yield strength by ~7-10% and compressive modulus by ~15-21% relative to NSF at nearly the same density, while NSF showed a higher peak stress; thicker-walled S60HS microspheres gave the best compression performance. A COMSOL FE model reproduced CWS60-30-B1 within ~8%.

extraction.paper_summary: Orbulov and Ginsztler produced three aluminium (Al99.5) matrix syntactic foams by pressure infiltration of randomly close-packed beds (~64 vol%) of ceramic hollow spheres of three sizes: SL150 (100 um), SL300 (150 um) and Globocer (1450 um). Quasi-static compression tests (14 mm diameter cylinders, H/D = 1, 1.5, 2; crosshead 0.15 mm/s; DIN 50134) were run at room temperature and at 220 C, tracking compressive strength, fracture strain, structural stiffness and absorbed specific energy. Smaller, thinner-walled microballoons gave higher compressive strength, higher fracture strain and (for SL300) higher stiffness; increasing aspect ratio lowered strength and energy absorption strongly for the SL foams but barely for Globocer; testing at 220 C dropped compressive strength by ~30-35% (still above 120 MPa) while raising fracture strain by ~5%.

extraction.extraction_notes:
IMPORTANT CAVEAT: this paper reports every mechanical property (compressive strength, fracture strain, structural stiffness, absorbed specific energy) only as bar/scatter plots in Figs 4-8. No table or sentence gives a numeric strength, stiffness, strain or energy value, so per the rules all mechanical property fields are null and only structural data (Table 2 and Table 3) were captured. The only mechanical numbers stated in text are qualitative or relative: SL150 is ~10% stronger than SL300; the strength drop between H/D=1 and H/D=2 is 'more than 30 MPa' for the SL foams; elevated-temperature strength dropped ~30-35% while remaining 'above 120 MPa'; fracture strain increased ~5%; the H/D increment reduced consumed energy by ~50% (SL) and 5-10% (Globocer). These are recorded in specimen_notes/evidence rather than as property values.

Record granularity: the study crosses 3 materials x 3 aspect ratios x 2 temperatures (Globocer at room temperature only), i.e. 15 nominal (composition x test condition) cells. Because no property values are readable, 15 records would differ only in the aspect ratio text, so 5 records were written (one per material x test temperature actually run) with the H/D range noted in specimen_notes. Re-extraction with figure digitisation would be needed for the 15-cell grid.

Unit/derivation notes: porosity converted from percent to fraction (e.g. 44.7% -> 0.447 for total porosity, kept in microstructure_notes; matrix_porosity_fraction uses the paper's signed matrix porosity, -6.3% -> -0.063, negative because measured density exceeded theoretical, meaning some microballoons were themselves infiltrated). particle_wall_thickness_ratio (eta = inner/outer radius) is not stated by the authors; it was computed exactly from the Table 2 average diameter and wall thickness (SL150: (50-3.69)/50 = 0.926; SL300: (75-6.75)/75 = 0.910; Globocer: (725-58)/725 = 0.920). particle_true_density_g_cc left null because Table 2 quotes 'density at 64 vol%' (the packed-bed density of the sphere assembly: 0.576 / 0.691 / 0.816 g/cm3), not the particle true density. Particle volume fraction 0.64 is the authors' stated nominal random-close-pack value ('~64 vol%'), not a measurement per block. particle_type set to ceramic_hollow because the authors call them ceramic microballoons/hollow ceramic spheres; the SL types are Envirospheres 'E-spheres', which are commonly fly-ash derived, but the paper never says fly ash, so fly_ash_cenosphere was not used. Strain rate left null: the crosshead speed of 0.15 mm/s is stated but the corresponding nominal strain rate differs per specimen height (0.0107, 0.0071, 0.0054 1/s for H = 14, 21, 28 mm) and these records merge the three heights. Room temperature entered as 25 C per the schema convention. Infiltration/processing temperature is not given numerically. Literature values quoted in the introduction (e.g. cp-Al foams >100 MPa, Al7075 foams up to 230 MPa from Balch et al.; Couteau and Dunand foams 1.2-1.5 g/cm3 crept at 500 C under 5-14 MPa) are other papers' results without full composition/test detail and were not turned into secondary records.

extraction.paper_summary: A review/short study from Moscow Power Engineering Institute on syntactic foams (hollow-microsphere-filled polymer coatings) used as thin-film thermal insulation for heat supply equipment and pipelines. It classifies insulating materials, compares aluminosilicate (fly-ash), solid/hollow glass and thermoplastic polymer microspheres, and reports measured thermal conductivity of one-layer syntactic foam coatings made with de-aerated (rarefied-air-filled) versus gas-filled hollow glass microspheres at 60 C and 100 C. The main finding is that coatings based on de-aerated hollow glass microspheres have roughly an order of magnitude lower thermal conductivity than gas-filled ones, while polymer microspheres are limited to ~90 C service temperature.

extraction.extraction_notes: Review-style paper with only one set of the authors' own quantitative measurements (thermal conductivity of one-layer syntactic foam coatings). OCR mangles degree signs: '+500C - +1200C' is the +50 to +120 C range, '600C'=60 C and '1000C'=100 C; temperatures were read accordingly. test_type set to 'other' because the measurement is steady-state thermal conductivity, not a mechanical test. Matrix/binder is never identified (the paper only says 'various binding agents'), so matrix_class='other' and matrix_name=null; process_route='other' since the coating application method is not described. Particle volume/weight fraction is not reported for the tested coatings. Table 1 (materials classification) and Table 3 (microsphere characteristics) contain no composite property data. Table 2 lists properties of conventional insulants (mineral wool, PU foam, foamed concrete, etc.), which are not hollow-particle composites, so no records were made from it. Fig. 1 values were not read off the plot; only the values stated in the text were used. Particle size and density ranges quoted in Sec. 4 are generic literature ranges for microsphere classes, not measurements on the tested coatings, so they were left null and only noted in microstructure_notes.

extraction.paper_summary: Tensile behaviour of syntactic foams made by injection moulding expandable PMMA-shell polymer microballoons (Expancel 950-120, ~120 um) into two PP/SEBS 70/30 blends (SEBS A = small 80-140 nm particles, SEBS B = large 200-250 nm particles) at 0-50 vol% microballoon, i.e. relative densities 0.5-1.0, tested at nominal strain rates of 1, 10 and 100 1/s. Apparent elastic modulus rises with strain rate (a drastic rise between 10 and 100 1/s, delayed by adding microballoons) while yield stress rises only slightly; ductility collapses as soon as any microballoons are added. PP/SEBS A foam moduli follow the Gibson-Ashby rho^2 law at 10 and 100 1/s whereas PP/SEBS B foams fall well below it, and both foams reach similar moduli regardless of matrix modulus.

structure.microstructure_notes: Relative density 0.98 (paper reports relative densities 0.5-1.0 for 0-50 vol% microballoon, and explicitly names relative density 0.98 for the 2 vol% blend and 0.9 / 0.8 foams). Expandable PMMA-shell microballoons, ~120 um mean diameter, ~0.1 um shell wall thickness; SEM shows de-bonding between microballoons and matrix.

test.specimen_notes: Injection-moulded plate 150 x 150 x 3 mm; ASTM micro tensile dumbbell, parallel portion width 4.8 mm, gauge length 22.2 mm; tensile axis along injection direction; nozzle 200 C, mould 40 C, injection pressure 75 MPa; three repeats averaged.

evidence.quote: Eight kinds of syntactic foams and one neat PP/SEBS specimen were prepared at same manufacturing process : 0, 2, 4, 8, 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 volume percentages of microballoons in each PP/SEBS blend matrix.

the nominal strain rates were 1, 10 and 100 s-1 in the PP/SEBS syntactic foams because of the limited number of syntactic foam specimens. Apparent elastic modulus, yield stress and strain energy up to failure were measured

The microballoon was Expancel grade 950 ~120 (Akzo Nobel) whose average diameter was about 120 um. The material of microballoon's shell was made of polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA). The average thickness of the microballoon's shell was about 0.1 um
The tensile mechanical properties of PP/SEBS blend syntactic foams with the relative densities from 0.5 to 1.0 are characterized at the nominal strain rates of 1, 10 and 100 s-1.

structure.microstructure_notes: Relative density 0.60 (paper reports relative densities 0.5-1.0 for 0-50 vol% microballoon, and explicitly names relative density 0.98 for the 2 vol% blend and 0.9 / 0.8 foams). Expandable PMMA-shell microballoons, ~120 um mean diameter, ~0.1 um shell wall thickness; SEM shows de-bonding between microballoons and matrix.

test.specimen_notes: Injection-moulded plate 150 x 150 x 3 mm; ASTM micro tensile dumbbell, parallel portion width 4.8 mm, gauge length 22.2 mm; tensile axis along injection direction; nozzle 200 C, mould 40 C, injection pressure 75 MPa; three repeats averaged.

evidence.quote: Eight kinds of syntactic foams and one neat PP/SEBS specimen were prepared at same manufacturing process : 0, 2, 4, 8, 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 volume percentages of microballoons in each PP/SEBS blend matrix.

the nominal strain rates were 1, 10 and 100 s-1 in the PP/SEBS syntactic foams because of the limited number of syntactic foam specimens. Apparent elastic modulus, yield stress and strain energy up to failure were measured

The microballoon was Expancel grade 950 ~120 (Akzo Nobel) whose average diameter was about 120 um. The material of microballoon's shell was made of polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA). The average thickness of the microballoon's shell was about 0.1 um
The tensile mechanical properties of PP/SEBS blend syntactic foams with the relative densities from 0.5 to 1.0 are characterized at the nominal strain rates of 1, 10 and 100 s-1.

extraction.extraction_notes: NO numeric property values could be extracted. Every mechanical result in this paper (apparent elastic modulus, yield stress, strain energy to failure, Gibson-Ashby and rule-of-mixtures comparisons) is presented only in Figs. 2-8, 11 and 12; the paper states no modulus, strength, strain or density number in the running text. Table 1 (SEBS grades) and Table 2 (foam compositions) are present in the PDF but their cells came through the text extraction empty ([TABLE p2-1] contains only captions), so nothing could be read from them. Per rule 2 all Properties fields are therefore null and no values were read off the plots. Records enumerate the (composition x strain rate) grid that was actually tested: 2 matrices x 9 microballoon volume fractions (0, 2, 4, 8, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 vol%) x 3 nominal strain rates (1, 10, 100 1/s) = 54 records. The 0 vol% rows are the neat PP/SEBS matrix baselines (the neat blends were actually swept over 0.3-100 1/s; only the three rates shared with the foams are recorded). Relative density is given in microstructure_notes rather than measured_density_g_cc because the paper never states an absolute density in g/cm3; relative density = 1 - microballoon volume fraction, which the paper itself confirms (2 vol% -> 0.98, and it discusses 0.9 and 0.8 foams). matrix_class = 'pp' for the PP/SEBS 70/30 blends (PP is the 70 vol% majority phase; the SEBS is part of the matrix blend, not a filler, so additional_fillers is null). particle_wall_thickness_ratio left null: the paper gives a ~0.1 um shell thickness on a ~120 um mean diameter but never reports a radius ratio, so no eta was derived. cure_or_process_temperature_c = 200 C is the injection nozzle temperature (mould 40 C, injection pressure 75 MPa). Test temperature not stated, left null.

extraction.paper_summary: Silicone-rubber (Smooth-On Mold Star 30) syntactic foams were hand-mixed and cast with 3M A16/500 (GB500) and A20/1000 (GB1000) glass bubbles at 10, 20 and 30 wt%, giving densities from 748 down to 360 kg/m3 versus 1120 kg/m3 for the neat resin (a 63-68% reduction at 30 wt%). Quasi-static compression was run at room temperature on virgin specimens and on specimens heat treated by holding one face at 500 C for 1 h. Increasing glass-bubble content raised the plateau stress and lengthened the plateau (crush) region, improving energy absorption, while the 500 C treatment produced a brittle heat-resistant surface layer (two-layer structure) without considerably changing the compression response.

evidence.quote: A syntactic foam was produced by mixing silicone rubber and glass bubbles by hand. After mixing for 20 min, the raw material was filled in a wax mold and compressed by hand. The specimen was designed to be cylindrical with a diameter of 25 mm and a height of 17 mm.

Compression experiments were performed by using Instron 5585 universal testing machine with a 1 mm/min cross head speed. Experiments were performed at room temperature for specimens with and without heat treatment.

structure.microstructure_notes: Closed-cell syntactic foam, glass bubbles dispersed in silicone rubber. After one-sided 500 C / 1 h exposure the foam becomes a two-layer structure: a white, brittle, heat-resistive front layer extending less than 1/3 of the section height and a back layer that stays elastic/plastic like the unheated foam; SEM shows the glass bubbles remain intact at 500 C (they rupture at 750 C). Steady-state back-face temperature 130 C.

extraction.extraction_notes: Densities converted from kg/m3 to g/cm3 (Table II divided by 1000). Weight percentages converted to fractions (particle_weight_fraction); volume fractions are not reported and were not computed because the paper does not give the resin density needed together with a stated mixing rule. All compression results (stress-strain curves, plateau stress, densification strain, energy absorption) appear only as plots in Figs. 2 and 4 with no numeric values in text or tables, so every Properties field is null; the records carry composition, density and test-condition metadata only. strain_rate_per_s = 0.00098 1/s was derived from the stated 1 mm/min crosshead speed and 17 mm specimen height (1/60 mm/s / 17 mm); it is not stated as a strain rate in the paper. cure_or_process_temperature_c is 25 C for the virgin foams (6 h room-temperature cure) and 500 C for the heat-treated foams (one face held at 500 +/- 10 C for 1 h); all compression tests themselves were done at room temperature, so test.temperature_c is 25 C for every record. The neat silicone rubber resin reference (1120 kg/m3) contains no hollow particles and was not recorded. The 0.06-0.16 W/(m K) thermal conductivity in Table I is a property of the glass bubbles quoted from the 3M datasheet, not a measured foam property, so it was not entered. Glass-bubble crush pressures (3.44 and 6.90 MPa) are supplier particle data and are recorded in particle_grade rather than as foam strength.

extraction.paper_summary: A literature/patent review (Modern Applied Science, 2015) of binding agents for syntactic foams - hollow-microsphere-filled composites - used as heat-insulating coatings on power-industry pipelines and equipment. It surveys patents combining glass, ceramic, polymer and fly-ash microspheres with acrylic latex, epoxy, polyurethane, silicone, liquid-glass, phosphate and cement binders, and tabulates the qualitative characteristics and thermal stability limits of thermoset, thermoplastic and inorganic binder classes. It concludes that organic/element-organic binders are limited to about 400 C while phosphate and aluminosilicate binders (stable to ~2000 C) are the most promising but under-studied.

extraction.extraction_notes: This is a REVIEW/patent survey; the authors report no measurements of their own. Every record is therefore data_origin='secondary', with the source patent or paper named in sample_label. Only rows of Table 1 and passages of Sec. 4 that state a numeric property were turned into records; Table 1 rows with purely qualitative outcomes (modified ash microspheres/polyurethane, latex-composite coating, epoxy 'high adhesion to a pipe', Lestosil silicone/boron nitride, metallised ceramic microspheres) were skipped, as were Tables 2 and 3, which describe binder chemistry and setting behaviour rather than foam properties. Many quoted properties are ranges (0.02-0.03, 0.16-0.175, 0.029-0.034 W/(m*K); 51-75 kg/m^3); those fields are left null with the range recorded in microstructure_notes, per the no-invented-numbers rule. Values stated as 'up to X' are recorded as X with a note. Unit conversions: breaking strength 2.4 kgf/mm^2 -> 23.5 MPa (x 9.80665); densities kg/m^3 -> g/cm^3 (51 -> 0.051, 400 -> 0.4, 600 -> 0.6). The '51kg/mm3' in Table 1 is a typographic error for 51 kg/m^3. Process route, particle size, particle loading, test standards, strain rates and test temperatures are not given for any composition, so those fields are null; process_route='other' throughout. Maximum service temperatures quoted in Table 1 (150 C, 600-650 C) are operating limits, not test temperatures, so they are kept in notes rather than test.temperature_c. Confidence is low-to-moderate on all records because they are unverified patent/advertising claims - the paper itself criticises the 0.001 W/(m*K) figure as unrealistic.

extraction.paper_summary: Microstructural (SEM, EDS map and line-scan, XRD) study of SL150, SLG and SL300 ceramic hollow microspheres (Envirospheres Ltd.) and of the Al99.5 and AlSi12 matrix syntactic foams made from them by pressure infiltration at ~60 vol% sphere content. The sphere wall consists of densely packed Al2O3 needles (5-10 um long, <0.5 um thick) embedded in a mullite plus amorphous SiO2 matrix, so SiO2-rich zones form at the sphere surface. In Al99.5 matrix foams the molten aluminium reduces this amorphous SiO2 (4Al + 3SiO2 -> 2Al2O3 + 3Si), producing gamma-Al2O3 and a degraded ~6 um interface layer that is expected to lower compressive strength, whereas in AlSi12 matrix foams (and in Al-SL300, infiltrated at the lower 690 C) the reaction is suppressed and the sphere walls stay intact with an interface layer under 3 um.

structure.microstructure_notes: Microsphere size distribution 56-183 um (95% range), specific surface 0.060 1/um. Sphere wall is Al2O3 needles (5-10 um long, <0.5 um diameter) embedded in a mixture of mullite and amorphous SiO2 (SEM/EDS maps). XRD phase content of the foam: Al 67, Si 8, mullite 11, alpha-Al2O3 3, gamma-Al2O3 11, quartz 0, amorphous 0 (wt%). Molten Al reduced the amorphous SiO2-rich zones (4Al + 3SiO2 -> 2Al2O3 + 3Si), producing gamma-Al2O3 and severely degrading the microsphere wall; EDS line scan shows a wide (~6 um) diffuse interface layer with poorly defined outer sphere edge. Particle porosity 50.9%, total porosity 44.7% (Tab. 2).

extraction.extraction_notes: This paper reports NO mechanical property measurements (no modulus, strength, energy absorption or hardness numbers), so all Properties fields are null; test.test_type is 'other' because only density/porosity, XRD, SEM and EDS characterisation were performed. data_origin is 'secondary' for all six records because Tab. 2 (theoretical and measured density, particle/matrix/total porosity) is explicitly labelled as taken from ref. [3] (Orbulov I., Dobranszky J., 'Producing metal matrix syntactic foams by pressure infiltration', Period. Polytech. Mech. Eng. 52(1), 2008, 35-42), which is cited in sample_label. The XRD phase data of Tab. 3 and the SEM/EDS observations are primary to this paper and are captured in microstructure_notes. Porosities converted from percent to fractions. matrix_porosity_fraction is NEGATIVE for the three Al99.5 foams (-0.062, -0.058, -0.072); the authors state a negative value means the microspheres themselves were partly infiltrated, so the calculated particle porosity is overestimated - it is not a physical negative porosity. Particle porosity (50.9/49.5/48.2%) and total porosity (44.7-52.0%) have no schema field and are recorded in microstructure_notes. particle_volume_fraction=0.60 from the stated '~60 vol%' and applies to all six foams. Infiltration temperature is given only for Al-SL300 (690 C, stated as the lower temperature that suppressed the reaction); it is null for the other foams. Sphere chemical composition in Tab. 1 is printed once and applies to all three SL grades. Test temperature set to 25 C as a default for room-temperature characterisation.

extraction.paper_summary: Metal matrix syntactic foams made by inert-gas (Ar) pressure-assisted liquid infiltration of Al99.5, AlSi12, AlMgSi1 and AlCu5 matrices around ceramic hollow spheres (Globocer, 1444 um; SL300, 150 um) at ~64 vol% random close packing were examined after quasi-static (0.01 1/s), split-Hopkinson high strain rate (933 and 2629 1/s) and cyclic compression (R=0.1, f=10 Hz, k=0.7-0.9). Quasi-static loading damages the foam by matrix plasticity with progressive sphere fracture and barrelling, whereas at high strain rate the spheres crack parallel to the load already at ~2.5% strain and fully disintegrate at 2629 1/s, splitting the specimen. Under fatigue the unalloyed Al99.5 matrix foams fail along a single ~45 deg shear band while the harder Si-alloyed AlSi12 foams fail in a lenticular zone between two compression cones, which the authors attribute to the relative yield strength of matrix and ceramic spheres.

extraction.extraction_notes: This is a purely microstructural/fractographic damage study: it reports NO measured mechanical property values (no modulus, strength, plateau stress, energy absorption or fatigue life numbers) in text or tables, so all Properties fields are null and the records carry composition, structure and test-condition metadata only. particle_volume_fraction=0.64 comes from the stated '~64%' random close packing value and applies to all foams. particle_wall_thickness_ratio was computed as eta=(D/2 - t)/(D/2) from Table 2 (Globocer: (722-58)/722=0.92; SL300: (75-6.75)/75=0.91); it is not stated directly in the paper. Engineering deformations quoted in the figures (2%, 2.45%, 8.12%, 10%, 30%, 60%) are the imposed sectioning strains, not strains at failure, so strain_at_failure was left null. Test temperature set to 25 C (quasi-static tests stated 'at room temperature'; the SHPB and fatigue tests are assumed room temperature). Records were created only for the (matrix x filler x test condition) combinations for which results are actually presented. The Materials section also lists AlSi12, AlMgSi1 (O and T6) and AlCu5 (O and T6) matrices with Globocer filler for the monotone compression tests, but the paper states the damage mechanism was 'very similar' and presents no separate data for them, so no records were created for those. Homogenisation 520 C/30 min (and 170 C/14 h T6 ageing for AlMgSi1 and AlCu5) is heat treatment after infiltration; the infiltration temperature is not given, so cure_or_process_temperature_c is null.

extraction.paper_summary: Finite-element (Abaqus/Explicit) study of aluminium (Al6061) automotive crash boxes (70 x 70 x 200 mm) filled with glass-microballoon/epoxy syntactic foam in six filling configurations (full, 1/2, 1/4, empty, 8 mm and 16 mm lateral wall thickness), impacted by a rigid wall at 64 km/h for 5 ms. No foams were manufactured or tested: the syntactic-foam elastic constants (density 0.3 g/cm3, E = 1650 MPa, nu = 0.2) and Johnson-Cook plasticity constants were taken from / fitted to literature data (Li et al., Mater. Sci. Eng. A 515, 19 (2009)). The FEA shows that increasing foam fill lowers crash-box displacement, that full filling gives the highest (undesirable) initial reaction force, and that lateral-wall foam filling (Cases 5 and 6) gives the best compromise of energy absorption and reaction force at little weight penalty.

extraction.extraction_notes: This is a pure finite-element / light-weighting design study; the authors manufactured and tested no syntactic foam themselves, so no primary Process-Structure-Property data exist. The only quantitative foam material data are the FE material cards in Tables III and IV, both attributed to ref. [11] (P. Li, N. Petrinic, C.R. Siviour, R. Froud, J.M. Reed, Mater. Sci. Eng. A 515, 19 (2009)); Table III is tagged data_origin='secondary' (values quoted from that paper) and Table IV 'model' (Johnson-Cook constants the present authors calculated/fitted). The paper states only 'micro glass bubble/epoxy' - no microballoon grade, volume/weight fraction, particle size or processing route is given, so those fields are null and process_route is set to 'other'. Table IV as printed has 6 parameter columns but only 5 numbers, so the exponent m is missing; A=15 MPa, B=0.01 MPa, n=0.0001, C=0.105, eps_dot_0=3500 1/s is the alignment implied by the running text. strength_mpa=15 records the Johnson-Cook A constant and should be treated as a constitutive parameter, not a measured strength; the test_type 'compression' and strain rate 3500 1/s reflect the reference strain rate of that card. extraction.paper_summary: Elastomeric syntactic foams made by mixing 3M A16 hollow glass microballoons (mean diameter 60 um) into Sylgard 184 PDMS at nominal volume fractions of 0.10, 0.20, 0.37 and 0.46 were compressed in situ inside an X-ray computed tomography scanner, with digital volume correlation and per-particle tracking used to follow microballoon collapse. Damage transitioned continuously from dispersed microballoon collapse at low volume fraction to clustered collapse forming 'pseudo crush bands' and fully collapsed pockets at high volume fraction, with collapse starting at eng. strain about -0.07 for phi = 0.46 versus only at large strains for phi = 0.10. Across all specimens the probability of microballoon survival fell as the local coordination number N_neighbor rose, so local particle clustering rather than global volume fraction best predicts damage.

extraction.extraction_notes: This is a damage-mechanism / in situ XCT imaging study, NOT a property-measurement study: it reports NO numeric mechanical property values for the foams. Engineering stress-strain curves (Fig. 2a), the fraction of intact GMBs versus strain (Fig. 2b), DVC strain fields (Fig. 4), clustering histograms (Fig. 5) and survival probabilities (Fig. 6) are shown only as figures, and the OCR'd text carries no axis values, so per rule 2 all Properties fields are null. The four records capture the four compositions (nominal phi = 0.10, 0.20, 0.37, 0.46) that were compression-tested, with the qualitative and semi-quantitative damage observations kept in microstructure_notes. matrix_class = 'other_thermoset' because the Sylgard 184 PDMS silicone elastomer has no dedicated enum value. cure_or_process_temperature_c = 25 C encodes 'cured at room temperature'. Test temperature and strain rate are not stated (loading was applied in 500 um displacement increments), so both are left null. Particle true density and wall-thickness/radius ratio are not reported. Reported strains such as -0.07, -0.14, -0.28, -0.30 and -0.44 are damage-initiation/imaging strains, not strains at failure, so strain_at_failure is left null and the values are recorded in microstructure_notes. Matrix moduli quoted from other papers in Sec. 5.1 (E_PDMS = 3 MPa [22], E_epoxy = E_vinylester = 3.0 GPa [23], E_PU = 250 MPa, E_PP = 21 MPa) are properties of neat matrix polymers, not of syntactic foams, so they were not turned into records. OCR caveat: the volume-fraction symbol phi is repeatedly garbled in the text extraction (rendered as '(/)', 'sck', '4)', '0'), and Sec. 3.1 twice refers to a 'phi = 0.07' specimen where the context makes clear the phi = 0.10 specimen is meant; the four nominal volume fractions were taken from Sec. 2.1 and the Fig. 1/3/4 captions, which agree.

extraction.paper_summary: HDPE (Braskem SHA7260, described as green polyethylene) syntactic foams filled with 1 and 5 wt% 3M iM16K hollow glass microspheres (0.46 g/cm3, 20 um, 16000 psi crush strength) plus a constant 5 wt% PE-g-MA compatibiliser were compounded by single screw and by co-rotating twin screw extrusion, compression moulded, and tested in tension (ASTM D638) and notched Izod impact (ASTM D256). SEM showed poor matrix/filler adhesion and incomplete wetting throughout, with the twin screw route giving better HGM dispersion but far more microsphere breakage and glass debris. Twin screw processing cut elastic modulus, tensile strength and strain by roughly 20, 10 and 23 %, and raising HGM from 1 to 5 wt% reduced properties further (5 % for modulus up to 50 % for strain); impact strength was the exception, rising 315 % for TS1 and 215 % for TS5 over the neat matrix while SS1 fell 12 %.

Elastic modulus (Fig. 4), maximum tensile strength (Fig. 6), strain at maximum strength (Fig. 7) and Izod impact strength (Fig. 8) are all shown only as bar charts with no axis values quoted in the text, and there is no property table. The text gives only PERCENTAGE CHANGES relative to the neat HDPE matrix, and the schema has no field for a relative change, so every Properties field is null per rule 2. The reported changes are preserved verbatim in the evidence quotes: twin screw processing reduced elastic modulus, tensile strength and strain by 20 %, 10 % and 23 %; increasing HGM content reduced properties by 5 % (modulus) up to 50 % (strain); strain at break fell 6.06 % (SS1), 50.73 % (SS5), 25.62 % (TS1) and 42.04 % (TS5) versus the matrix; Izod impact strength changed by -12.17 % (SS1), +315.13 % (TS1) and +215.35 % (TS5). 7 records = 4 formulations (SS1, SS5, TS1, TS5) x tension, plus 3 impact records - SS5 has no impact record because the paper states its impact performance 'was not assessed due to the equipment limitations'. No neat-HDPE baseline record was created: the matrix is used as the 100 % reference in every figure but is not listed as a processed formulation in Table 1 and no numbers are given for it. Only weight fractions are reported (1 and 5 wt% HGM, 5 wt% PE-g-MA); particle_volume_fraction is left null - it was NOT converted, because although the HDPE (0.955 g/cm3) and iM16K (0.46 g/cm3) densities are given, the paper never reports a foam density and the PE-g-MA/HDPE split would have to be assumed. process_route='extrusion' covers the compounding step that distinguishes the samples (single vs twin screw); the test specimens were subsequently compression moulded at 180 C, which is recorded in specimen_notes. cure_or_process_temperature_c is the top of the extruder temperature profile: 150 C for the single screw samples (140-150 C) and 190 C for the twin screw samples (170-190 C). Tensile temperature_c=25 encodes the paper's 'at room temperature'; the impact test temperature is not stated and is left null. Strain rate is null for the tensile tests: the crosshead speed (50 mm/min) is given but the gauge length is not, so no 1/s value could be derived. Inconsistency worth flagging: the title, abstract and keywords call the matrix 'green polyethylene' (Braskem's sugarcane-derived PE), but Sec. 2.1 identifies it only as HDPE grade SHA7260 with no bio-based content stated. Also note a stray sentence in Sec. 3.2.1 referring to 'better performance for LMS', an undefined acronym that appears nowhere else.

extraction.paper_summary: 7055 Al-alloy matrix syntactic foams reinforced with 1-2 mm Al2O3 hollow particles (52 vol.%) were made by simple gravity infiltration casting at 740, 770, 800 and 830 C, then normalized, annealed, quenched or solution-aged (470 C/1 h base). Average foam density was 1.73 g/cm3 with 40.89 % porosity. Quasi-static compression (1e-3 /s) gave the best as-cast properties at 800 C infiltration (yield 78.23 MPa, compressive strength 79.52 MPa, plateau 26.6 MPa); solution-aging gave the highest strength (95.32/96.45 MPa) and normalizing the best plateau stress (78.63 MPa) and energy absorption (48.14 MJ/m3, 28.04 kJ/kg).

The 39-46 % porosity in Table 5 is the total foam porosity contributed by the hollow particles, not unintended matrix voids, so matrix_porosity_fraction is left null and the value is recorded in microstructure_notes. Particle volume fraction 0.52 is stated once in Sec. 3.3 ('the hollow particle volume fraction was 52 %') and applied to all primary samples. Particle true density is left null: Table 2 gives only a manufacturer range (bulk density 0.5-1 g/cm3); particle diameter is left null because only a 1-2 mm screened range is given, no mean. Test temperature recorded as 25 C for 'ambient temperature'. The 20 Table 8 comparison rows are literature values from other papers, marked data_origin='secondary' with the cited reference in sample_label; only density and energy absorption are given there (specific energy absorption in kJ/kg has no schema field, so it is kept only in the evidence quote). extraction.paper_summary: Al 7075 matrix syntactic foams filled with recycled expanded-glass (EG) spheres of 0.5-1, 1-2 and 2-4 mm were produced for the first time on a fully automated industrial cold-chamber high-pressure die casting machine, and the casting parameters (casting temperature, injection pressure, piston speed, filler preheat temperature, piston waiting time) were optimised for each filler size. Nine flawless 60 x 80 mm cylinders were cast with densities of 1.82-2.06 g/cm3 (mean 1.93), EG volume fractions of 34.5-45.6 % and total porosities of 27.2-35.9 %. Smaller EG spheres gave lower density and higher porosity but needed higher injection pressure, piston speed, preheat and waiting time; injection pressure and piston speed were the most influential parameters on density, which rose to as much as 2.14 g/cm3 when they were raised. The study is fabrication/characterisation only - no mechanical tests were run.

records.sample_label: SF1

processing.particle_grade: recycled expanded glass (EG) spheres, Omnis Composite Ltd; 73 wt% SiO2, 14 wt% Na2O, 8 wt% CaO, 4 wt% MgO, 0.15 wt% Al2O3, 0.1 wt% Fe2O3; size range 0.5-1 mm

structure.microstructure_notes: Total porosity 33.8 % (= 0.338 as a fraction), calculated from Eq. (3) as the EG volume fraction times (1 - rho_fil/rho_solid); this is the intended porosity contributed by the porous EG spheres, not unintended matrix voiding, so it is reported here rather than in matrix_porosity_fraction. EG spheres have a thin-walled outer surface and a porous inner structure; supplier bulk density 0.2-0.35 g/cm3 and thermal conductivity 0.065 W/mK (particle property, not the foam). Optical/SEM images show metallic matrix plus porous EG spheres with secondary phases: combined/agglomerated particles, broken sphere fragments and matrix-filled spheres; small shrinkage cavities can form at the matrix/filler interface and molten Al can partially penetrate EG pores, raising density.

test.specimen_notes: Cylindrical casting 60 mm diameter x 80 mm length, cold-chamber high-pressure die casting (die and sprue preheated to ~300 C, solidification ~30 s). Optimised parameters for this filler size: injection pressure 210 bar, piston speed 40 mm/s, EG preheat 600 C, piston waiting time 30 s, casting temperature 730 C. Characterisation only: density by mass/cylindrical volume, EG volume fraction and total porosity from Eqs. (1)-(3), plus optical and SEM microscopy. No mechanical testing was performed in this paper, hence test_type='other'.

extraction.extraction_notes: This is a processing/characterisation paper: it reports NO mechanical or thermal property of the foams, so every Properties field is null in all records. All ten records therefore carry test_type='other' with specimen_notes explaining that only density, volume fraction, porosity and microscopy were measured. Records 1-9 are the nine foams of Table 2 (verbatim density, EG volume fraction converted from % to fraction, total porosity). Record 10 is the 2.14 g/cm3 maximum density stated in the Conclusions for the extra 2-4 mm samples of the Fig. 8 injection-parameter series; its process point is only shown graphically, so confidence is low and volume fraction/porosity are null. particle_type='other' rather than 'ceramic_hollow' or 'glass_microballoon': the expanded-glass granules are millimetre-scale porous (foamed) glass spheres with a thin dense outer skin, not hollow-shell microballoons; 'ceramic_hollow' would be the nearest enum if a hollow-particle class must be assigned. particle_mean_diameter_um is the arithmetic midpoint of the paper's stated size band (0.5-1 mm -> 750 um, 1-2 mm -> 1500 um, 2-4 mm -> 3000 um); the paper reports only ranges, never a mean, so treat these as derived. particle_true_density_g_cc left null: the paper quotes 0.2-0.35 g/cm3 as the supplier BULK (poured) density of the EG granules, which is not the particle true density. Total porosity is placed in microstructure_notes, not matrix_porosity_fraction, because it is the intended porosity of the EG filler (Eq. 3) rather than unintended matrix voiding. process_route='pressure_infiltration' is the closest enum value; the actual route is industrial cold-chamber high-pressure die casting, in which a piston pressure-infiltrates molten Al into a preheated bed of EG spheres (die/sprue preheated ~300 C). cure_or_process_temperature_c is the casting temperature: 730 C for the 0.5-1 and 1-2 mm foams and 720 C for the 2-4 mm foams, per Sec. 3.3. NOTE an internal inconsistency - Sec. 3.1 states 'all the casting processes, regardless of filler size, were carried out at 730 C', which contradicts the 720 C given in Sec. 3.3 for the 2-4 mm foams; Sec. 3.3 was followed as it is the size-specific statement. A second internal inconsistency: Sec. 3.2 says foam density AND total porosity both rise with EG sphere size, but Table 2 (and the Conclusions) show porosity FALLS as sphere size rises; Table 2 numbers were taken as authoritative. A third: the Conclusions call 45.6 % the 'highest porosity value' of SF3, but 45.6 % is SF3's EG volume fraction - its total porosity is 35.9 %; Table 2 was followed. Table 1 (process trials P1-P10 for the 1-2 mm filler) was transcribed but generates no records because no density or property value is reported per trial - only a pass/fail visual assessment in Fig. 3. The P10 combination (730 C, 200 bar, 30 mm/s, 550 C preheat, 20 s) is recorded in specimen_notes for the 1-2 mm foams as the stated optimum.

extraction.paper_summary: This paper documents the conservation and restoration of a polychrome (painted) wooden coffin from the Dahshur archaeological area, Egypt, dating to the Late Period. It covers documentation, wood identification (Faidherbia albida), insect/microbial sterilization with nanochitosan, mechanical and chemical cleaning, reattachment of gesso layers with Paraloid B72, and consolidation of the painted layer with calcium oxide nanoparticles in Klucel G. Glass microballoons mixed with Paraloid B72 and earth pigments were used only as a gap-filling paste for the edges of the ground layer.
extraction.extraction_notes: Off-topic for syntactic foams. The only mention of hollow particles is the use of glass microballoons combined with Paraloid B72 in acetone (15 W/V) as a restoration filling material for cracks/voids at the edges of the gesso ground layer of an archaeological wooden coffin. No composition series, no volume/weight fractions, no mechanical, thermal or physical property measurements of a hollow-particle composite are reported anywhere in the paper. Therefore is_syntactic_foam_paper=false and records is empty.

extraction.paper_summary: Orbulov and Majlinger characterise the microstructure of SL150 and SL300 ceramic hollow microspheres (Envirospheres Ltd.) and of the aluminium matrix syntactic foams (MMSFs) made from them by pressure infiltration with Al99.5, AlSi12, AlMgSi1 and AlCu5 matrices at ~60 vol% microspheres. SEM plus map and line EDS show the microsphere wall is built from Al2O3 needles (5-10 um long, <0.5 um diameter) embedded in a mullite + amorphous SiO2 matrix, and that molten aluminium reduces the SiO2-rich zones (4Al + 3SiO2 -> 2Al2O3 + 3Si), degrading the sphere wall and forming gamma-Al2O3. The reaction was intensive with Al99.5, AlMgSi1 and AlCu5 matrices but suppressed with AlSi12 (high matrix Si lowers the driving force) and for Al99.5-SL300 infiltrated at the lower temperature of 690 C; interface layers were ~2-4 um (AlMgSi1), ~3 um (AlCu5) and <1.5 um (AlSi12), with Mg dissolving into the wall for AlMgSi1 and CuAl2 precipitating on it for AlCu5. The paper reports no mechanical property measurements.

extraction.extraction_notes:
IMPORTANT CAVEAT: this is a purely microstructural/analytical paper (SEM, map and line EDS, XRD). It contains NO mechanical, thermal or physical property measurements of the foams, so every field in Properties is null in all eight records. The records capture the processing and structure data (matrix, microsphere grade and size, volume fraction, densities, porosities, XRD phase constitution, matrix-particle reaction state) for the eight matrix x microsphere combinations.

data_origin: the density and porosity values in Table 2 are explicitly cited to reference [3] (I. N. Orbulov, J. Dobranszky, Periodica Polytechnica Mechanical Engineering, 52(2008)35-42), the same authors' earlier paper, so all eight records are marked 'secondary' with that citation in sample_label. The XRD phase constitutions of Table 3 and all EDS/SEM observations were measured in this paper (primary) and are recorded in microstructure_notes rather than as separate records.

Unit conversions: porosity percentages converted to fractions for matrix_porosity_fraction (e.g. -6.2% -> -0.062). Matrix porosity is negative for the Al99.5, AlMgSi1 and AlCu5 foams because the measured density exceeded the theoretical one, which the authors attribute to microspheres that were themselves infiltrated. Note an internal inconsistency: the text says 'the values of matrix porosity are always remained below 8%' while Table 2 lists -13.4% (AlMgSi1-SL150) and -12.2% (AlCu5-SL300); Table 2 values were used as printed. Table 2 here also differs slightly from the same data in the authors' companion paper (W136470296): matrix porosity -6.2 vs -6.3% for Al99.5-SL150, and theoretical density 1.42 vs 1.41 g/cm3 for Al99.5-SL300.

particle_volume_fraction = 0.60 comes from the text ('The volume fraction of the microspheres was maintained at relatively high (~60 vol%) level'); it is a nominal target, not a per-block measurement. The 50.9% / 48.2% values in Table 2 are the porosity contributed by the hollow interiors, not the sphere volume fraction, and are kept in microstructure_notes. particle_true_density_g_cc and particle_wall_thickness_ratio are null because Table 1 of this paper gives average diameter, size range and specific surface but no wall thickness or density. cure_or_process_temperature_c is filled only for Al99.5-SL300 (690 C, the only infiltration temperature stated numerically); the others are described only as higher. test_type is 'other' (density / XRD / SEM-EDS characterisation, no mechanical loading) and test temperature is left null since none is stated. Quartz content is given as 1 wt% and mullite 19 wt% in Table 1 of this paper (the companion paper quotes 15-20% mullite and 0-5% quartz ranges). Literature results cited in the introduction were not turned into records.

extraction.paper_summary: Orbulov studies the pressure-infiltration production of aluminium metal matrix syntactic foams (MMSFs) made from AlSi12 alloy and SLG-type ceramic hollow microballoons (E-spheres, Envirospheres) tapped to ~64 vol%. A purpose-built, thermally controlled infiltration rig was used to measure the infiltrated length as a function of Ar gas pressure (0.5-4 bar) and infiltration time (1-5 s) at ~640 C melt temperature. The measured threshold pressure lay between 0.5 and 1 bar, supporting the Kaptay capillary model over the Trumble and Rohatgi models, and the infiltrated length grew with a time exponent of ~1.5-2.7 rather than the theoretically predicted square-root dependence.

records.sample_label: AlSi12 + SLG E-spheres (64 vol%), pressure infiltration

structure.microstructure_notes: Microballoon chemistry 36-40 wt% Al2O3, 55-60 wt% SiO2, 1.4-1.6 wt% TiO2, 0.4-0.5 wt% Fe2O3; average outer diameter 130 um and average wall thickness ~5.4 um (calculated by the author from the real density of the microballoons and the density of their wall). Microballoons were poured into a 10 mm OD / 1 mm wall, 150 mm long 316L stainless tube and tapped rigorously to reach a randomly close packed ~64 vol% (R-CPES), versus 74 vol% for ideal close packing. Possible interfacial reaction 4Al+3SiO2=3Si+2Al2O3 (dG ~ -300 kJ/mol at 700-850 C) noted at longer infiltration times.

The measured quantity is the infiltration length L (mm) of the AlSi12 melt into the tapped microballoon bed, under Ar pressure of 0.5-4 bar for 1-5 s, melt superheated to melting point + 70 C (thermocouple T4 = 640 C in all runs). Measured L: 0 mm at 0.5 bar / 5 s; 17, 29, 41, 68 mm at 1-4 bar for 1 s; 21, 41, 54, 95 mm at 1-4 bar for 3 s; 43, 71, 94, 146 mm at 1-4 bar for 5 s. Threshold pressure between 0.5 and 1 bar. These infiltration-length values have no field in this schema.

extraction.extraction_notes: This is a genuine syntactic-foam paper (aluminium matrix syntactic foam, hollow ceramic microballoons) but it is a PROCESSING/INFILTRATION-KINETICS study only: it reports no mechanical, thermal or density properties of the produced foam. Every field in Properties and in Structure density is therefore null. Only ONE record is emitted because the material system is fixed (AlSi12 + 64 vol% SLG E-spheres) and the variables the paper sweeps - infiltration pressure (0.5-4 bar) and infiltration time (1-5 s) - have no representation in this schema; emitting 13 records would produce 13 identical rows. The 13 measured infiltrated lengths and the fitted power-surface coefficients (Tables 1-4) are recorded verbatim in test.specimen_notes rather than being forced into an unrelated schema field. Unit conversions: particle real density 640 kg/m3 -> 0.64 g/cm3; volume fraction 64 vol% -> 0.64. particle_wall_thickness_ratio left null: the paper gives outer diameter (130 um) and wall thickness (5.4 um) but never states the inner/outer radius ratio, so it was not derived. particle_type set to ceramic_hollow following the paper's own wording ('ceramic hollow microballoons'); note that Envirospheres E-spheres are fly-ash derived, and the stated Al2O3/SiO2 chemistry is cenosphere-like, but the paper never calls them fly ash. Test temperature 640 C is the matrix thermocouple reading T4, constant across all runs. Threshold-pressure model equations (Kaptay, Trumble, Rohatgi) and Fig. 1 are analytical predictions of pressure, not of any schema property, so no 'model' records were created.

extraction.paper_summary: Six metal matrix syntactic foams (MMSFs) made by pressure infiltration of ~64 vol% ceramic hollow microspheres (E-spheres SL150 / SLG / SL300, mean diameters 100 / 130 / 150 um) with Al99.5 or AlSi12 aluminium matrices were characterised by three hardness methods: global (Brinell) hardness, quasi-static depth sensing hardness and dynamic (Equotip) hardness. Global hardness rose above the matrix value for Al99.5 foams and fell below it for AlSi12 foams, and was nearly matrix-independent, so it is a structural property; the smallest spheres (SL150) always gave the highest global and dynamic hardness. Depth sensing tests revealed the 4Al+3SiO2 -> 2Al2O3+3Si exchange reaction that degrades the microsphere walls in Al99.5 foams, absorbed energy was mostly plastic and varied linearly with the loading slope, and cross-sections showed damage localised directly under the imprints.

structure.microstructure_notes: Pressure-infiltrated block, as-fabricated. Reported porosities (image analysis, Table 2): total 44.67%, 'planned' (hollow-microsphere) 50.86%, 'unwanted' -6.18%. Microspheres are E-spheres (Envirospheres Pty. Ltd.), specific surface 0.06 1/um, composition 30-35% Al2O3, 45-50% amorphous SiO2, 19% mullite, 1% quartz, bal. other. Originally broken spheres removed by a buoyant method. matrix_porosity_fraction left null because the reported unwanted porosity is negative (-6.18%): the authors state the infiltration pressure broke some microspheres and their interiors were infiltrated, so the image-analysis value is not a physical void fraction. Exchange reaction 4Al(liq)+3SiO2(sol) -> 2Al2O3(sol)+3Si(sol) degraded the microsphere walls in the Al99.5 matrix foams (strongest for SL150 and SLG).

test.standard: EN ISO 6506:2005 (Brinell global hardness); ASTM 956-96 (Equotip dynamic hardness); depth sensing hardness test is not standardised
test.specimen_notes: Three hardness tests on each block, 10 measurements each: (1) global Brinell hardness, 10 mm hard steel ball, 1839 N (187.5 kp) for Al99.5 foams and 2452 N (250 kp) for AlSi12 foams, 10 s dwell, imprints ~0.2 mm deep; (2) quasi-static depth sensing hardness on an MTS 810, 2.5 mm hemispherical mandrel to 1600 N at 0.02 mm/s, imprints ~0.4 mm deep with a ~0.5 mm affected zone; (3) dynamic hardness with an Equotip device, 5 g indenter, HD = 1000*va/vb HL. Block size 35 x 55 x 170 mm.

The microspheres were compacted by gently tapping. By this way ~64 vol% of microspheres can be incorporated.

extraction.extraction_notes: All hardness results (Fig. 3 global hardness, Figs. 6 and 7 absorbed elastic/plastic/total energies, Fig. 10 dynamic hardness) are plotted only - no numerical hardness or energy values appear in the text or tables - so no property values could be extracted without reading them off the plots, which the prompt forbids. Additionally, the schema has no hardness field (Brinell HBS, depth sensing, Leeb HL) and no field for indentation absorbed energy in J, so even tabulated values could not have been stored in Properties. The extractable quantitative data are therefore composition, processing and structure: microsphere grade, mean diameter and specific surface (Table 1), porosities (Table 2), ~64 vol% microsphere loading, infiltration temperature (600 C for AlSi12, 710 C for Al99.5) and pressure (0.4 MPa for 30 s). One record per produced block type (6 blocks) rather than per hardness method, because no measured value distinguishes the three test conditions; test_type is 'other' since hardness/indentation is not in the TestType enum. particle_volume_fraction 0.64 is the authors' stated packing of the microsphere bed, not a per-block measurement; note that Table 2 lists a 'planned porosity' of 48-51% which is the internal void volume of those spheres, not the sphere volume fraction. For the Al99.5 blocks the reported 'unwanted' porosity is negative (-5.80 to -7.19%) because infiltration broke and filled some microspheres, so matrix_porosity_fraction was left null there and the value recorded in microstructure_notes; the AlSi12 blocks use the reported positive values (1.13-2.03%). Only relative statements are given for hardness (matrices differ by ~40 HBS globally and ~30% dynamically, the latter dropping to ~15% for the foams; AlSi12 foams absorbed ~2.5x more indentation energy than the pure matrix), so these are left in the summary.

extraction.paper_summary: Higuchi, Adachi, Yoshioka and Yokochi fabricated functionally graded syntactic foams by dispersing acrylonitrile hollow microballoons (Matsumoto Microsphere MFL-100CA, 80-110 um, 130 +/- 30 kg/m3) in a bisphenol-A epoxy (AER2603 / Rikacid MH-700 / jER BMI12, 100:86:1) and letting the balloons float during pre-cure, either from a uniformly dispersed state (TF = 65 C, tF = 2 h) or from a two-phase separated state (TF = 50 C, tF = 50 min), then pre-curing at 100 C for 2 h and post-curing at 130 C for 15 h. Density graded continuously from ~1200 kg/m3 (pure epoxy layer) to ~500 kg/m3 (maximum balloon packing); DMA (10 Hz, tension, 25-220 C) showed that the temperature dependence of the moduli and the 175 C glass transition are controlled by the epoxy matrix and are independent of balloon content. Quasi-static compression of specimens cut from the graded foams showed that compressive Young's modulus (~0.5 to ~2.1 GPa) and yield stress (~20 to ~110 MPa) depend only on local density (quadratic Gibson-Ashby type relation), independently of fabrication route or mould geometry.

extraction.paper_summary: Yu, Qian, Liang & Li (Ceramics-Silikaty 60(1) 77-84, 2016) is a purely numerical (ANSYS 14.0 finite-element) study of the effective elastic modulus of hollow-glass-microsphere/epoxy syntactic foams reinforced with randomly oriented short glass fibres, using 180 x 180 x 180 um representative volume elements built by random sequential adsorption. Six microsphere volume fractions (5-30 %), six relative wall thicknesses eta = 0.02-0.12 and three fibre volume fractions (2, 4, 6 %) were simulated under 1 % compressive strain. The modulus falls with increasing microsphere content below a critical relative wall thickness of 0.04-0.05 and rises above it, a kink/maximum appears near eta = 0.06 at 25 vol.% microspheres, adding glass fibres raises the modulus and lowers the critical wall thickness, and the peak von-Mises stress sits on the microsphere equator perpendicular to the loading direction, moving onto the fibres as the wall thickens.

extraction.extraction_notes: This is a purely numerical (FEM/RVE) paper on hollow glass microsphere + short glass fibre epoxy syntactic foams; no specimens were made or tested, so no primary data exist. Every composite result is reported ONLY as a normalised relative modulus E/Em plotted in Figures 2-5 (six microsphere volume fractions 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 %; six relative wall thicknesses eta = 0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08, 0.10, 0.12; fibre volume fractions Vf = 0, 2, 4, 6 %). No E/Em value is stated numerically in the text or in any table, so per the extraction rules none of those ~144 modelled conditions could be turned into records without reading values off plots - they are all omitted rather than estimated. The single record kept is the model's unfilled epoxy matrix input (Em = 3 GPa = 3000 MPa, rho = 1.16 g/cm3) from Table 1, marked data_origin = model; it is the normalising baseline for every figure. Other Table 1 inputs, recorded here only in notes: hollow glass microsphere E = 70 GPa, nu = 0.20, rho = 2.18 g/cm3, diameter 50 um; glass fibre E = 73 GPa, nu = 0.20, rho = 2.18 g/cm3, diameter 16 um, length 80 um. Qualitative numeric findings without extractable property values: critical relative wall thickness 0.04 with fibres and 0.05 without; modulus maximum near eta = 0.06 at Vs = 25 %; maximum 4.8 % deviation between free and periodic boundary conditions at Vs = 30 %. No process route applies (simulation), so process_route = other.

extraction.paper_summary: Russian-language VIAM paper (Chursova, Sokolov, Lukina, 2017) describing two new lightweight core materials for aircraft sandwich structures: a closed-cell syntactic foam (spheroplastic) grade VPZ-17 made from a high-deformability cyanate-ester binder (VST-1210, an aryl dicyanate oligomer plus cycloaliphatic epoxy) filled with hollow glass microspheres (grades MS-VP / MS-VP-A9), and a chemically blown phenolic-rubber foam grade VPP-4 (not a hollow-particle composite). The syntactic foam is produced by blending binder with microspheres, calendering into <=2 mm sheets, cutting and molding plates; it has a density of 0.67 g/cm3 and retains useful strength up to 160-180 C. Reported spheroplastic values: 33/31 MPa tensile, 92/63 MPa compressive and 80/54 MPa flexural strength at 20/160 C.

extraction.extraction_notes: Paper is in Russian; 'сферопластик' (spheroplastic) = syntactic foam. Six records extracted from Table 1 (grade VPZ-17), one per test type x test temperature (20 C and 160 C). Only strengths and bulk density are reported; no moduli, strains, volume/weight fractions, particle size or particle density are given anywhere in the paper, so those fields are null. Density 0.67 g/cm3 is listed only in the 20 C column and was carried over to the 160 C records as the material's density. The Charpy impact toughness (5,5 kJ/m2 at 20 C, GOST 4647-49) and the dielectric permittivity data (2.07 as-received, 2.27 after 30 days at 98% RH, 2.13 after 1 day drying, at 10^10 Hz) have no matching schema fields and were therefore not turned into records. Table 2 reports properties of sandwich panels (glass- or carbon-fibre skins over the spheroplastic core: densities 1.2 and 1.0 g/cm3; tensile 250/220 and 340/360 MPa; compressive 315/270 and 323/238 MPa; flexural 531/507 and 697/483 MPa at 20/160 C) - these are multilayer structures, not the hollow-particle composite itself, so they were excluded. Table 3 (phenolic foams FK-20 and VPP-4, densities 190-230 and 80-150 kg/m3) describes chemically blown closed-cell foams with no hollow particles and was excluded as out of scope. Process route recorded as compression_molding: binder + microspheres were mixed, calendered into sheets <=2 mm, cut and then molded into plates; no cure temperature was given for the spheroplastic.

extraction.paper_summary: LSU doctoral dissertation (Manu Kuruvila John, 2009) proposing a shape memory polymer (SMP, polystyrene-based, with carbon nanotubes) matrix syntactic foam containing glass microballoons, used as the core of an orthogrid-stiffened composite sandwich structure for self-healing (self-sealing) of low velocity impact damage. The foam and sandwich were characterized by DSC, TEM, SEM, thermal conductivity, flat-wise compression, low velocity impact (30 J and 53 J) and compression-after-impact, with strain-controlled thermomechanical programming at 3% and 20% prestrain and 2-D/3-D confined shape recovery. The authors report repeatable sealing over 7 impact-healing cycles with healing efficiency above 100%.

IMPORTANT COVERAGE CAVEAT: the supplied text file data/text/W2728148627.txt is truncated. It contains only PDF pages 1-40 of a 118-page dissertation and stops mid-way through the introduction of Chapter 2. All of the author's own quantitative results are therefore absent from the text: Table 1 (thermal conductivity and specific heat), Table 2 (elastic constants and Poisson's ratio of the foam phases), Tables 3-5 (low velocity impact results at 30 J and 53 J for 3% and 20% prestrain), Table 6 (uniaxial compressive yield strength after post-curing), and all figures with stress-strain and CAI data are not present in the file. No [TABLE]...[/TABLE] blocks exist in the file at all. Consequently NO primary records could be extracted for this paper; re-extraction from the full PDF is strongly recommended.

The two records above are SECONDARY values quoted in the dissertation's literature review from Kishore et al. (ref. [9]). The paper states only the two endpoints of a linear trend (2 GPa and 2.47 GPa, converted to 2000 and 2470 MPa) versus microballoon volume fraction; the actual volume fractions, matrix chemistry and processing route of that cited study are not given here, so matrix_class and process_route are set to 'other' and volume fraction is left null. Test type inferred as tension because the cited work concerns tensile strength and fractography.

Other numbers seen in the available text but deliberately NOT turned into records because they are generic class-wide upper bounds rather than a specific composition x test condition: 'syntactic foams display uniaxial compression strengths up to 100 MPa, hydrostatic compression strengths up to 150 MPa, uniaxial tension strengths up to 25~30 MPa and tensile Young's modulus up to 2500~3000 MPa' (Sec. 1.1, citing ref. [7]). Impact energies (30 J, 53 J), prestrain levels (3%, 20%) and the >100% healing efficiency claim appear in the abstract but with no accompanying material property values in the available text.

extraction.paper_summary: Four thin heat-insulating syntactic-foam coatings based on a water dispersion of an acrylic polymer filled with hollow microspheres were sprayed onto glass plates and characterised for structure (light microscopy), thermal conductivity (TCi modified transient plane source analyser, ISO 22007-2:2015) and infrared thermography: SFC-1 and SFC-2 with 60 and 80 vol.% alumino-silicate ceramic spheres (1-40 um) and SFG-1 and SFG-2 with 80 vol.% glass spheres (9-25 um and 20-80 um). Coating density fell from 315 to 125 kg/m3 with filler type and loading, and the coating thermal conductivity ranged from 0.029 W/(m*K) (SFC-1) to 0.205 W/(m*K) (SFG-2). The best insulation came from 60 vol.% ceramic spheres of 1-40 um and from 80 vol.% fine glass spheres of 9-25 um (both R = 0.008 (m2*K)/W); raising the ceramic sphere content from 60 to 80 vol.% left the spheres unenveloped by the unchanged binder amount and increased k about four-fold.

extraction.extraction_notes: Only thermal data are reported - no mechanical testing - so all Properties fields except thermal_conductivity_w_mk are null. Unit conversions: coating densities converted from kg/m3 to g/cm3 (315 -> 0.315, 215 -> 0.215, 125 -> 0.125, 165 -> 0.165); microsphere loadings converted from vol.% to fractions (60% -> 0.60, 80% -> 0.80). matrix_class set to 'other_thermoplastic' for the acrylic-polymer water dispersion (no acrylic entry in the MatrixClass enum); process_route set to 'other' - the coatings were spray-applied in two layers with a spray gun, the second layer after 6 h of room-temperature drying, so no numeric cure temperature is given. test_type set to 'other' because transient-plane-source thermal conductivity is not in the TestType enum, and the test temperature is not stated (the 15 C room / 45 C plate / 65 C source values belong to the separate infrared thermography setup, not to the TCi measurement). Only size ranges are given for the microspheres, never a mean diameter, so particle_mean_diameter_um is left null and the ranges recorded in microstructure_notes. Discrepancies in the source: the running text of Sec. 3.2 gives k = 0.089 W/(m*K) for SFG-1 while Table 2, the abstract and the same paragraph's comparison give 0.087 - the table value 0.087 was used; and Sec. 3.1 gives the SFG-2 sphere size as 20-90 um while Table 1 gives 20-80 um. The equivalent conductivity keq, the thermal resistance R and the infrared thermography results (Table 3: dt, Dtmax, D at 16.7 C) have no schema fields and were placed in microstructure_notes; infrared thermography was not made into separate records because it yields no schema-mappable property value. Reference conductivities quoted from the literature (glass plate 1.18 W/(m*K) [14], acrylic matrix 0.2 W/(m*K) [15]) are not foam data and were not extracted.

extraction.paper_summary: Chordiya and Goel (2019) report a purely numerical LS-DYNA study of the drop weight impact hammer test on a polymeric syntactic foam (epoxy matrix with 60 vol% hollow glass particles and 5 vol% nanoclay), both as bare foam and filled inside an aluminium tube. Three foam densities (220, 320, 460 kg/m3), three drop velocities (3.13, 4.42, 6.26 m/s corresponding to 0.5, 1 and 1.5 m drop heights and nominal strain rates of 30, 40 and 60 /s) and two foam material models (MAT_063 crushable foam and MAT_024 piecewise linear plasticity) give 36 simulations. Peak stress and energy absorption rise with foam density and impact velocity, and filling the foam into a tube raises reaction force and energy absorption (about 4-12%) while lowering peak stress in the foam by 5-15% and reducing displacement.
